analysis.one_liner: Bars gun and ammunition sales to anyone convicted of a violent misdemeanor in the past five years.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: all 13 of its House supporters were Democrats, it sat in the House Judiciary Committee for a year before moving to a subcommittee, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime for anyone to sell or hand over a firearm or ammunition to a person convicted in any court of a violent misdemeanor within the previous five years. It defines "violent misdemeanor" narrowly, requiring use, attempted use, threatened use, or intentional causing of physical injury, and it includes protections for people whose convictions lacked a lawyer or a jury trial or were later expunged. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never advanced to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People at risk of gun violence, especially in communities where guns bought shortly after a violent offense are used in shootings, and law enforcement, which gains a federal tool to stop those sales.

how_it_helps.text: Adds a new prohibited-purchaser category: no firearm or ammunition may be sold or otherwise given to anyone convicted of a violent misdemeanor in the preceding five years.
Covers people convicted under federal, state, tribal, or local law, closing gaps where a violent conviction under one jurisdiction's law would not bar a purchase under another's.
Adds the new prohibition to the background-check system used by licensed dealers, so a check would flag a disqualifying recent violent misdemeanor conviction before a sale.

Includes due-process limits: a conviction only counts if the person had counsel or validly waived it, and where a jury trial was available, if the case was tried by a jury or the person validly waived one; expunged, pardoned, or rights-restored convictions do not count.

analysis.who_pays: Gun dealers and sellers, who would lose some sales and face an expanded background-check requirement, and people with recent violent misdemeanor convictions, who would be unable to buy a gun or ammunition for five years.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun sellers and recent violent offenders

drawbacks.text: The prohibition on "sale or other disposition" applies to every seller, but background checks are only required of licensed dealers, so the bill does not require checks on private sales and enforcement against private transfers would be limited.

A five-year bar is triggered by a misdemeanor conviction, which even with the bill's violence element and due-process safeguards could catch people whose offense caused relatively minor injury, and gun-rights critics argue it penalizes a constitutional right based on a non-felony record.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety gain is targeted and real but modest: it applies only to people with a violent misdemeanor conviction in the last five years, not a lifetime ban, and the due-process carve-outs limit the chance of sweeping in people wrongly convicted. The cost falls on gun sellers in lost sales and paperwork. The main weakness is enforcement, since private sales without background checks remain possible under current law.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee when introduced, sat there for nearly a year before being referred to a subcommittee on crime, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Joe Neguse introduced the bill on November 4, 2021, joined by eight other House Democrats, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
Twelve other House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
On November 1, 2022, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, the last action of record before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun sellers are better off, because the proposed bar on selling to people with recent violent misdemeanor convictions never became law; nothing about who can buy a gun changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun sellers, whose sales rules stayed the same

for.name: Joe Neguse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for nearly a year without a hearing or markup, then referred it to a subcommittee, where it remained until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat: 13 House Democrats total, with no Republicans signing on and no record of Republican support.

industries.note: The bill would create a new class of prohibited purchasers, cutting off sales to people convicted of a violent misdemeanor in the past five years and adding the category to dealer background checks. The industry's interest in keeping those customers runs against the safety benefit to the public.
